title: Tourism has several effects

blocks.heading: Tourism has several effects
blocks.text: Tourism can create demand for local work and supplies while placing pressure on water, land, services and cultural life. Trace the mechanism and who gains or bears costs. A visitor count alone cannot establish net local development.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Effects on people
blocks.text: Tourism can provide jobs, skills and exchange, but can also produce seasonal work, rising local costs or unwanted intrusion. Outcomes depend on participation, conditions and community influence. Avoid treating residents as a single group with identical gains.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Economic effects
blocks.text: Tourist spending can support incomes and suppliers when local workers, owners and producers participate and retain earnings. Imported supplies or profits sent elsewhere reduce some local links; uncertain demand and seasonality can make earnings unstable.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Environmental effects
blocks.text: Tourism can finance conservation or create incentives to protect habitats, but can also increase waste, water demand and disturbance. Visitor management, maintained facilities and meaningful local participation affect the balance. A protected-area label alone does not establish sustainable use.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Compare impacts
blocks.text: Describe this original fictional tourism comparison: A retains N$60 of each N$100 visitor spending locally and uses 40 water units per visitor; B retains N$20 and uses 70. A combines greater local retention with lower water demand: N$40 more retained and 30 fewer water units per visitor. The two measures favour A on those criteria, without a complete net-impact verdict.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Connect this lesson to Production (3.1), Sustainable Development (1.2) and Urbanisation (4.2). Identify the livelihood or resource constraint, trace the mechanism and distinguish a feasible action from a hoped-for outcome. The cases here are fictional, not claims about a named present-day community.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
